content: Routine monitoring of gastric residuals in preterm infants receiving tube feeds is a standard practice in neonatal intensive care units. This practice is used to guide the initiation and progression of enteral feeding. However, there is no clear consensus on whether the aspirated gastric residuals should be re-fed to the infant or discarded. Re-feeding gastric residuals may potentially support digestion and enhance gastrointestinal motility and maturation by reintroducing partially digested milk, gastrointestinal enzymes, hormones, and trophic substances. On the other hand, abnormal gastric residuals could lead to complications such as vomiting, necrotizing enterocolitis, or sepsis. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of re-feeding gastric residuals compared to discarding them in preterm infants. A systematic search was conducted in February 2022 using databases such as Cochrane CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL. Additional searches included clinical trial registries, conference proceedings, and reference lists of relevant articles. The study focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared the two approaches. The selection criteria included RCTs that directly compared re-feeding versus discarding gastric residuals in preterm infants. Data collection and analysis were performed by two independent reviewers who assessed trial eligibility, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data. Treatment effects were analyzed for individual trials, with results reported as risk ratios (RR) for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences (MD) for continuous outcomes, both with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The GRADE approach was used to assess the certainty of the evidence. The review identified one eligible trial involving 72 preterm infants. Although the trial was unmasked, it was otherwise methodologically sound. The findings suggested that re-feeding gastric residuals may have little or no effect on the time to regain birth weight (MD 0.40 days, 95% CI −2.89 to 3.69; 59 infants; low-certainty evidence). Similarly, re-feeding may have little or no effect on the risk of necrotizing enterocolitis (stage ≥ 2) or spontaneous intestinal perforation (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.25 to 2.04; 72 infants; low-certainty evidence), all-cause mortality before hospital discharge (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.14 to 1.85; 72 infants; low-certainty evidence), or the time to establish enteral feeds of ≥ 120 mL/kg/day (MD −1.30 days, 95% CI −2.93 to 0.33; 59 infants; low-certainty evidence). Additionally, there was little or no effect on the number of days of total parenteral nutrition (MD −0.30 days, 95% CI −2.07 to 1.47; 59 infants; low-certainty evidence) or the risk of extrauterine growth restriction at discharge (RR 1.29, 95% CI 0.38 to 4.34; 59 infants; low-certainty evidence). The effect of re-feeding on the number of episodes of feed interruption lasting ≥ 12 hours was uncertain (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.52; 59 infants; very low-certainty evidence). In conclusion, the review found limited data from a single small unmasked trial on the efficacy and safety of re-feeding gastric residuals in preterm infants. The available low-certainty evidence suggests that re-feeding gastric residuals may have little or no impact on key clinical outcomes, including necrotizing enterocolitis, all-cause mortality before hospital discharge, time to establish enteral feeds, duration of total parenteral nutrition, and in-hospital weight gain. A larger, well-designed randomized controlled trial is necessary to provide more definitive evidence on the efficacy and safety of re-feeding gastric residuals in preterm infants, which could help inform clinical policies and practices.
